key_terms.meaning: Any potential cause of harm to a cloud asset.
A weakness in code, configuration or process that a threat can exploit.
Risk = likelihood × impact of a threat exploiting a vulnerability.
The path an attacker uses to reach and exploit a target.
Two tenants' virtual machines running on the same physical host.
A bucket or volume left publicly readable or writable by mistake.
Threat checklist: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
Only authorised parties can read the data.
Data is not altered without detection.
Proving that a principal is who it claims to be.
A party cannot deny having signed or sent a message.
Message Authentication Code: a keyed checksum that proves integrity and authenticity.
Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data: one algorithm gives confidentiality and integrity.
A chain of keys: root key → key-encryption key (KEK) → data-encryption key (DEK).
Encrypt data with a DEK, then encrypt the DEK with a KEK.
Replacing sensitive data with a non-sensitive token that maps back only in a vault.
Granting only the permissions a task actually needs.
One trusted identity provider vouches for a user across many cloud services.
Breaking out of a guest virtual machine onto the hypervisor or host.
Security Information and Event Management: collects and correlates logs and raises alerts.

takeaways: Cloud security is shared: the provider hardens the platform, while the customer owns identity, configuration and data.
A threat needs a vulnerability and a path; closing any one of the three removes the risk.
Confidentiality, integrity, authentication and non-repudiation each need a different mechanism, and each fails differently in the cloud.
Encryption is only as strong as the key hierarchy and who holds the root key.
Data protection follows the data lifecycle: classify, control access, encrypt or redact, retain, then delete or archive safely.
IAM is the main control plane in the cloud; least privilege and short-lived credentials cut most attack paths.
MFA strengthens one login, SSO reduces repeated logins, and federation moves the trust decision to one identity provider.
Hypervisor isolation is necessary but not sufficient; shared hardware, images and migration paths need their own controls.
Monitoring gives evidence, auditing proves control, and incident response is a repeatable loop: prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn.
Cloud bursting and secure interfaces keep identity, data and traffic controlled when a workload crosses a trust boundary.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to match each threat to a control, trace the key hierarchy from root key to data key, and show IAM policy plus monitoring as one closed loop.

bank.q: Define threat, vulnerability and risk. Explain how the three combine when a cloud storage bucket is left public.
outline: Threat is a potential cause of harm; vulnerability is a weakness; risk = likelihood × impact.
A public bucket is a misconfiguration (vulnerability); scraping bots are the threat; data exposure is the risk.
Controls: block public access, IAM policy, encryption, access logging.
Removing any one factor removes the risk.

bank.q: Explain confidentiality, integrity, authentication and non-repudiation. Name one mechanism for each and one cloud failure mode for each.
outline: Confidentiality via encryption; integrity via hash, MAC or AEAD; authentication via password, MFA or certificate; non-repudiation via digital signature.
Cloud failure modes: weak key custody, silent tampering, credential theft, disputed API calls with no logs.
One mechanism can serve two goals, as AEAD does for confidentiality and integrity.
Match the mechanism to the goal.

bank.q: Describe the STRIDE threat model. Give one cloud example for each letter.
outline: Expand each letter: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
Examples: stolen token, altered bucket object, missing logs, public snapshot, traffic flood, over-broad IAM role.
Use STRIDE as a design-review checklist.
Map each threat to a control.

bank.q: What is a key hierarchy in cloud encryption? Explain root key, KEK, DEK and key rotation.
outline: Root key lives in an HSM or key management service; KEK protects DEKs; DEK protects data.
Envelope encryption flow: data → DEK → KEK → root key.
Key custody: provider-managed versus customer-managed keys.
Rotation re-wraps DEKs; deleting the root key crypto-shreds the data.

bank.q: Define IAM. Explain authentication versus authorization with a cloud example.
outline: IAM decides which authenticated principal may perform which action on which resource under which conditions.
Authentication proves identity; authorization checks permission.
Policy elements: principal, action, resource, condition.
Explicit deny wins; least privilege applies.
Example: a role may read one bucket only from one private endpoint.

bank.q: A team stores customer KYC scans in an object bucket. Design a data protection plan across the data lifecycle.
outline: Classify KYC scans as sensitive personal data.
Encrypt at rest with a customer-managed key; enforce TLS in transit.
Restrict access with IAM and a private endpoint.
Run DLP checks and redact fields before analytics.
Set a retention schedule and legal hold.
Delete securely and log every access.

bank.q: A company wants single sign-on for 20 SaaS apps and MFA for administrators. Design the authentication architecture.
outline: One identity provider is the source of truth.
Federate with SAML or OIDC; use SSO for the SaaS apps.
Enforce MFA for administrators and risk-based MFA for users.
Use conditional access based on device and location.
Set session lifetime and central logout.
Keep one break-glass account offline.

bank.q: Design secure isolation for multi-tenant virtual machines running on shared hosts.
outline: Patch the hypervisor and use hardware virtualization features.
Segment tenant networks with VLANs or overlay networks and security groups.
Harden images and use measured boot or vTPM.
Encrypt live migration and snapshots.
Mitigate side channels: core pinning, cache flushing, dedicated hosts for high assurance.
Test isolation with escape attempts and audits.

bank.q: Design a cloud bursting pattern for a retail sale peak while keeping identity and data secure.
outline: Define the trust boundary between private and public cloud.
Use federated identity and short-lived tokens; no shared long-term keys.
Connect with VPN or a dedicated link and use mTLS between services.
Encrypt data in sync; move only the minimum data.
Filter egress and monitor cross-boundary traffic.
Apply auto-scale policy and tear down burst resources after the peak.

bank.q: Set up monitoring and incident response for a cloud account.
outline: Collect control-plane, data-plane and access logs.
Track metrics for CPU, authentication failures and API errors.
Correlate in a SIEM and raise alerts.
Runbook stages: prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn.
Measure MTTD and MTTR.
Hold a post-incident review.

bank.q: Compare the security responsibilities of IaaS, PaaS and SaaS customers.
outline: IaaS: provider secures hardware, hypervisor and network; customer secures OS, apps, IAM and data.
PaaS: provider secures runtime and middleware; customer secures app, identity and data.
SaaS: provider secures most of the stack; customer secures users, configuration and data sharing.
Identity and data remain customer duties in all models.
Misunderstanding the split is itself a risk.

bank.q: "The hypervisor is the only isolation boundary that matters in the cloud." Evaluate this statement.
outline: Hypervisor is a key boundary but not the only one.
Co-residency side channels can cross it.
The management plane and APIs can bypass guest isolation.
Network segmentation, IAM and image security also matter.
Defence in depth: test isolation and audit.
Conclude that isolation is layered.

bank.q: Evaluate whether encryption alone protects data in the cloud.
outline: Encryption protects content, not metadata or access rights.
Key custody decides who can decrypt.
Authorised misuse still reads data.
Tokenization and redaction reduce exposure.
Retention and deletion complete the lifecycle.
Conclusion: encryption is necessary but not sufficient.

bank.q: A public bucket leaked customer data. Analyse which controls failed and what monitoring would have detected it.
outline: Bucket policy removed access control; public-access block was off.
No DLP scan on stored data.
Logging existed but no alert on public ACL changes.
Detection: configuration rule, access anomaly, SIEM correlation.
Response: revoke access, rotate keys, notify, learn.
Preventive control: policy as code and guardrails.
